Object data: All object data from the Met collection API object 329081 (date ca. 3100-2900 BCE, Jemdet Nasr period, Sumerian, clay, 5.4 x 6 x 4.1 cm, accession 1988.433.1, credit line 'Purchase, Raymond and Beverly Sackler Gift, 1988'). The Met records only 'Mesopotamia' as geography, so no find-spot coordinates are given; if a geo position is required, Uruk (Wikidata Q168518, 31.3259, 45.6374), the main source of proto-cuneiform tablets, is a defensible approximation but should be labelled as such.

madeIn.name: Southern Mesopotamia (find-spot unrecorded; placed at Uruk)

location.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

object.medium: Clay, impressed with a stylus and a cylinder seal
object.description: A small clay tablet recording the distribution of barley in the pictographic proto-cuneiform script, the earliest stage of writing in Mesopotamia. Numerical notations are pressed into the clay with the round end of a stylus beside signs for the commodity and its recipients. The reverse and edges were rolled with a cylinder seal showing a man with hunting dogs and boars.
facts: Dated by the Met to about 3100-2900 BCE, the Jemdet Nasr period, when writing was still largely pictographic.
The tablet measures 5.4 by 6 by 4.1 cm and entered the Met in 1988 as a Raymond and Beverly Sackler gift purchase.
Proto-cuneiform tablets are almost all administrative records, listing goods, rations and labour rather than language as speech.
